items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI says its AI cracked 3 major open problems in math, computer science, and...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI says its AI cracked 3 major open problems in math, computer science, and physics at once.

• The math result claims to prove "local smoothing" for waves in every dimension, which would settle the Kakeya, Stein restriction, and Bochner-Riesz conjectures together
• That would turn Hong Wang's 3D Kakeya proof, which won a Fields Medal this year, into a special case
• The CS result refutes the exponential time hypothesis, the belief that problems like 3-SAT always take exponential time
• Hundreds of papers rely on that assumption, and OpenAI says the proof was checked in Lean
• The physics result claims existence proofs for 4D Yang-Mills, QCD, and a grand unified theory, but not the mass gap needed for the $1M Millennium Prize
• A group led by Nobel laureate David Gross is reviewing the physics proof, and its materials haven't been released
• OpenAI says it won't seek academic credit for discoveries made by its internal models

@theojaffee: "Don't defer to the experts on releasing materials. You can defer to them on how you should communicate your results, but I don't see any legitimate reason for academics to block the result of a major math or science thing just because they want to."

Introducing Genie 4 from @GoogleDeepMind, our most realistic and interactive world model yet 🌍

Now ...
items.content:
Introducing Genie 4 from @GoogleDeepMind, our most realistic and interactive world model yet 🌍

Now you can use natural language to dynamically steer the world and its soundscape in real-time, whether you're changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing new elements to the environment.

So, how does the model do that?

Behind the scenes, Gemini acts as the "brain" of the simulation. It translates your requests into actions, plans out complex events, watches the scene unfold to keep track of what's happening, and adjusts as you change the story. Genie 4 also introduces ambient audio and real-time interactive human dialogue that adapts on the fly.

items.title: I think it's vastly underrated how important org chart and team functionality is to building a good ...
items.content:
I think it's vastly underrated how important org chart and team functionality is to building a good LLM. Over 18 months old, and still one of my favorite all time Interconnects posts. It's why we still often see orgs crumble and need to get rebuilt (e.g. Llama/xAI) and why I believe underdogs can still catch up. Having an effective org and team is worth multiple multiples in compute. 

I also think there isn't that much secret sauce to building models. Yes, sure there are some tricks, but most of the gains come from consistent execution and using your compute wisely.

items.content:
SF Compute CEO @evanjconrad advises AI founders to raise 10X more capital than planned, potentially $1 billion, just to secure compute:

"I would raise as much money as I can. I would take your round and I would add 10X to it. And if I was an investor, I would buy compute instead."

"I would either try to find a big investment grade normal company that I can partner with and use their balance sheet to co-sign on the lease with me, or I would try to raise the biggest round I possibly can, so I’m above the bar."

"If you’re trying to raise a round, I think you should try and raise like a billion dollars. I know. That’s the problem. This is why the article was called End of Startups. I don’t think many people can raise a billion dollar round."

"If you don’t fix the debt problem, most of the portfolios of various venture firms are gonna consolidate or get wiped out, or they will convert into basically GPU clouds."
@sfcompute

items.title: Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.7-Preview takes #2 on AA-Image-Editing v2.1, close behind OpenAI's GPT Image...
items.content:
Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.7-Preview takes #2 on AA-Image-Editing v2.1, close behind OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst (max) and a clear step up from MAI-Image-2.6

MAI-Image-2.7-Preview is Microsoft AI's newest image editing model, succeeding MAI-Image-2.6, released in August.

In our testing, MAI-Image-2.7-Preview scores higher than MAI-Image-2.6 on all 7 editing actions we measure, and ranks #1 on 4 of them: Scene & Style Edit, Text or Symbol Edits, Reasoning-Based Edit, and Enhancement & Restoration. This new model improves on MAI-Image-2.6 with the biggest gains in Composition & Framing (+57 Elo), Text or Symbol Edits (+49) and Scene & Style Edit (+48). We see its best use cases to be in Live-Action Film, Consumer and Frontier edits, where it ranks #1.

MAI-Image-2.7-Preview is available today in MAI Playground for image editing only, with text to image stated to be coming soon.

Congratulations to @MicrosoftAI on the release!

See below for our detailed analysis and example outputs of MAI-Image-2.7-Preview in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google DeepMind just launched Genie 4, a world model that builds interactive worlds you can walk into, with sound.

• You describe a scene or upload a photo, and Genie 4 generates a world you can move through in real time
• It now generates its own audio, from ambient sound and music to characters that talk back
• You can reshape the world mid-session with text, like changing the weather or adding a person
• Google is also using it to simulate robot tasks, like Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid playing checkers
• Google says visuals and object permanence can still drift during longer sessions
• It's a research preview for now, coming first to Google AI Ultra subscribers through a waitlist

@theojaffee: "I predict that I’m going to use these things basically as much as I use LLMs today."

1. "The benchmark owners alread...
items.content:
I've seen a lot of pushback to this, with the following complaints:

1. "The benchmark owners already know about the flaws, and are working on it."
2. "Why are they spending time critiquing and not contributing to the benchmark" OR "critiquing known issues are not helpful".
3. "The flawed verdict is too binary"

I find this pushback to be misguided.  These benchmarks are used to move millions of dollars of token spend, and many people blindly trust how well these benchmarks generalize to their own products, and don't look any further than the headline numbers.

For example, whenever a new model drops, you'll find thousands of youtube videos analyzing the pareto frontier using one of these benchmarks as the primary quality metric without questioning the benchmark.

I think we would all be better served by inviting skepticism and encouraging people to develop an independent opinion of how well these benchmarks represent the tasks they care about.  Concretely:

- For the failing tasks within the benchmark, are they: realistic, have a proper harness, graded properly, sufficiently disambiguated user intent?
- Are models and API calls configured properly (ex: inconsistent context windows, reasoning levels). 
- Are the models equipped with a modern harness and minimal retrieval that is sufficiently realistic?
- Does the score even make sense ex: is it just a LLM judge committee that produces a score on a 0-100 scale that isn't aligned with ground truth?

It's often the case you'll see many of these issues while looking at traces of a failing benchmark tasks, and it doesn't take long! Often the **very first trace you look at** has a serious issue.

I also don't think there is an issue with verified vs. flawed verdict.  It's good to have opinions.  If you look through enough of what's behind their opinions and you find that you usually agree with their verdict, then they have earned your trust, the same way that a benchmark can lose your trust.  

I think this eval of benchmarks is a red pill that motivates investing in your own private evals.

"Most AI labs t...
items.content:
SF Compute CEO @evanjconrad reveals why the world's AI compute is already sold out:

"Most AI labs think, I’m being asked for a really big prepayment by all of these different clouds. It must be because I don’t have leverage or I’m not a good negotiator."

"What they don’t know is, no, the cluster you’re buying does not exist. All the clusters that have been built are sold. That cloud has to go get debt for that new cluster."

"Most AI labs don’t connect the I have to do a big prepayment to the debt markets are freezing up. But it’s one-to-one."

"You can still get some Hopper, and you can still get some Ampere. But if you want Blackwells, yeah, they’re sold out. In part because the Blackwells weren’t made until you ordered them. Very few people speculatively built Blackwells. Lots of people speculatively built Hoppers."

"In Hoppers, the cloud builds a cluster, then the cloud sells the cluster. Blackwells, the customer signed a contract, then the cloud built the cluster. So every Blackwell cluster, for the most part, is spoken for."
@sfcompute

items.title: Ling 3.1 Flash 1019, an open weights model and successor to Ling 3.1 Flash, scores 44 on the Artific...
items.content:
Ling 3.1 Flash 1019, an open weights model and successor to Ling 3.1 Flash, scores 44 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, up from 41

@AntLingAGI has released Ling 3.1 Flash 1019, an update to Ling 3.1 Flash, their reasoning model with 560B total parameters, 25B active parameters, and a 1M token context window. It scores 44 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, up from 41 from Ling 3.1 Flash. Like Ling 3.1 Flash, Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 is open weights.

Key results:

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash 1019’s agentic capabilities improve over Ling 3.1 Flash. On AA-Briefcase v1.1, Ling 3.1 Flash 1019’s Elo is 1521, up 124 points from 1397 for Ling 3.1 Flash. Its Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1 is 1653, up from 1617 for its predecessor, an increase of 36 points. On AutomationBench-AA, Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 scores 68%, a 6 point increase from Ling 3.1 Flash’s score of 62%

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash 1019’s makes gains in scientific reasoning compared to its predecessor. Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 scores 43% on Humanity’s Last Exam, a 4-point improvement from 39% for Ling 3.1 Flash. It scores 26% on CritPt, an 8-point increase from 18%.

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 uses more output tokens per task than Ling 3.1 Flash. Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 uses 145k Output Tokens per Intelligence Index Task, more than 40% higher than Ling 3.1 Flash’s per task usage of 103k output tokens

➤ At $1.49 Cost per Task, Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 is more expensive than Ling 3.1 Flash but scores higher on intelligence. This is primarily driven by the higher number of output tokens used. However, Ling 3.1 Flash 1019  is still less expensive than models such as Mistral Large 4 Preview and GLM 5.3

Additional model details:

➤ Size: 560B total parameters, 25B active

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $0.90 per 1M output tokens, with cached input at $0.06 per 1M (80% discount)

➤ License: MIT

➤ Availability: Ling-3.1-flash-1019 is available as an open weights model on Hugging Face, and is accessible through InclusionAI’s first party API

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: An early Anthropic employee says a co-founder got upset about office sushi nigh...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: An early Anthropic employee says a co-founder got upset about office sushi night: "We’re not here to get rich and eat caviar."

• Ivan Vendrov joined Anthropic in October 2022, when it was about 40 people on 2 floors of an office in San Francisco’s Financial District
• His recruiter asked if he’d pledge to donate 2/3 of his equity, and it felt "a bit ambiguous" whether the offer depended on his answer, so he said yes
• At lunch, one employee said everyone was there because of AI x-risk, and a teammate replied that some just thought the tech was cool, which led to an awkward pause
• A senior colleague floated a new team to train dangerous bio, cyber, and nuclear models and show scary demos to governments
• When he said he’d rather work on beneficial deployments, his manager told him: "We are going to build AGI. And we’re going to do it safely."
• He quit after 8 months, before his equity cliff, when Anthropic was valued at around $4B

@theojaffee: "We’re not here to get rich. Oops. Well, now all the co-founders are gonna be worth probably about $50 billion at IPO."

items.content:
SF Compute CEO @evanjconrad explains why Anthropic winning the AI race could spell disaster for GPU cloud providers:

"I don’t think the clouds are gonna blow up suddenly or AI is doomed. But it doesn’t matter what I think. It matters what a lender thinks."

"Their biggest customers are ones who themselves want to be the GPU cloud. The frontier labs, the hyperscalers, the people who have investment-grade credit, will simply try to disintermediate you if they have the opportunity to."

"What if Anthropic just wins, and the clouds can’t sell to Anthropic because Anthropic just wants to do this, and they’re stuck selling to these other competitors who might die."

"Is that true? I don’t think that’s necessarily true. But this is the scenario that people are worried about."
@sfcompute

items.title:
the hex team consistently gets what it means to build agents, and software to support them

three th...
items.content:
the hex team consistently gets what it means to build agents, and software to support them

three things that caught my eye from Hex 4.0 that mirror what we've done at LangChain and that I think speak to the future of building agents

1/ use code as a backbone. they moved from yaml to more flexible code. agents are really good at writing code, and people want lots of flexibility in UI, so i think we will see more teams have parts of their UI that are powered by code. We did this in LangSmith with Custom Apps (completely custom UI)

2/ UX focused on reviewing. "A new, intuitive Hex UI, built for reviewing and understanding". As agents do more work, the bottleneck becomes reviewing work. We did a similar thing in LangSmith with our new Trajectory view, focused on being a new view over agent trajectories that make it easy to review

3/ rebuilt core infra. "An all-new, ridiculously faster execution engine". agents will still use infra/software. and it will need to be faster/better to accomodate more usage. We did this in LangSmith with SmithDB, our custom database for agent traces

I think all these three things (lets agents write custom UIs as code, invest in UI/UX that make it easier to review, make your core infra more scalable) are all generalizable to any company building agents

congrats to Hex team on a great milestone and great launch!

items.title: ARC Prize President @GregKamradt explains why Astra scoring 99% on ARC-AGI-3 doesn't mean AI has ach...
items.content:
ARC Prize President @GregKamradt explains why Astra scoring 99% on ARC-AGI-3 doesn't mean AI has achieved AGI:

"Astra was very good at ARC-AGI-3 using one of OpenAI’s harnesses. It got something like 99%, so more or less it saturated the benchmark."

"The reason why is because ARC-AGI-3 games had a finite ceiling. There was one answer to go and do. You didn’t have to produce anything along the way."

"Each one of the games were simple. A human can do them in five to 10 minutes. We tested 500 humans on ARC-AGI-3, so we have human baselines."

"ARC-AGI-3 was a really good stepping stone in the journey of expanding the diversity of environments. But it was a stepping stone, not the final thing."
@arcprize

items.title:
We've been running a few agents to monitor production systems for a few weeks now.

Agents working 2...
items.content:
We've been running a few agents to monitor production systems for a few weeks now.

Agents working 24/7, looking at failures, suggesting potential causes, and recommending fixes.

We're not only saving a ton of money, but we are also doing things we couldn't before.

But to set this up, you need to trust these agents. Here are a few questions you need to answer:

• Do your agents understand how your systems work?
• Can they see what actually happened?
• Do they have access to the code that changed recently?
• Can you verify the evidence behind the agent's recommendations?
• Do these agents recognize when they need help?

You can't automate production monitoring without all of this.

We've been running a few agents to monitor production systems for a few weeks now.

Agents working 24/7, looking at failures, suggesting potential causes, and recommending fixes.

We're not only saving a ton of money, but we are also doing things we couldn't before.

But to set this up, you need to trust these agents. Here are a few questions you need to answer:

• Do your agents understand how your systems work?

• Can they see what actually happened?

• Do they have access to the code that changed recently?

• Can you verify the evidence behind the agent's recommendations?

• Do these agents recognize when they need help?

You can't automate production monitoring without all of this.

items.title: Cartesia Managed Agents scores an Elo of 1115 on the Artificial Analysis Speech Agent Arena, 98 poin...
items.content:
Cartesia Managed Agents scores an Elo of 1115 on the Artificial Analysis Speech Agent Arena, 98 points above Cartesia's earlier voice agent product, Cartesia Line, with Task Success Rate up from 77.5% to 91.7%

Managed Agents is @CartesiaAI's fully managed platform for building and deploying voice agents. It is a cascaded system: Cartesia's own Ink Speech to Text and Sonic Text to Speech models run around an LLM of the developer's choice. We evaluated Cartesia Managed Agents with GPT-5.5 as the LLM and the Skylar and Daniel voices.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech Agent Arena: Cartesia Managed Agents scores an Elo of 1115 (95% CI 1086-1144, 685 samples), 98 points above Cartesia Line at 1017 (95% CI 985-1049)

➤ Agentic tasks: On tasks that need tool calls, Cartesia Managed Agents scores an Elo of 1112

➤ Task Success Rate: 91.7% of eligible tool-calling conversations end with the correct final task-completing tool call

Congrats to the @CartesiaAI team!

See below for more details ⬇️

items.title: ARC Prize President @GregKamradt reveals how Astra invented its own programming language to score ne...
items.content:
ARC Prize President @GregKamradt reveals how Astra invented its own programming language to score nearly 99% on ARC-AGI-3:

"At our ARC-AGI-3 launch in March, we had Sam Altman on stage to do a fireside with François. The moderator said, how long do you think it’ll take? And François’ answer was, well, it depends how much the labs make it a priority."

"We don’t have any concrete proof or evidence, but there’s an open question as to how much targeting was actually done on it. That’s the name of the game when you do these types of benchmarks."

"When Astra played this, it made its own domain-specific language on the fly. It created its own little code language for itself. That was something we hadn’t seen from models beforehand."

"Back in May, the models at that time thought they were playing Tetris. They thought they were playing Frogger. And then they tried to execute actions like they were playing those other games."

"Astra didn’t do that at all. Astra was much more aware about its novel environment."
@arcprize

SF Compute CEO @evanjconrad explains why GPU clusters are bad collateral for lenders:

"This article...
items.content:
SF Compute CEO @evanjconrad explains why GPU clusters are bad collateral for lenders:

"This article was more of a prediction of a trend that is already happening. I probably should’ve said, currently, most startups cannot buy compute. It is only getting harder and harder and harder."

"If you want to finance a GPU cluster, you need to first have collateral, which is typically the hardware itself. The problem with that collateral is nobody wants to buy the hardware. They want to buy the hardware in a data center that’s operated by a company that works."

"And the situation in which you recoup that hardware is often the situation in which the person operating that hardware is just as likely to blow up. There’s a lot of correlated risk."

"If you are the startup trying to buy a cluster, to the eyes of a lender, you look like you’re gonna blow up."
@sfcompute

items.title: FCC Chairman @BrendanCarrFCC warns superintelligence could supercharge cyberattacks on America's net...
items.content:
FCC Chairman @BrendanCarrFCC warns superintelligence could supercharge cyberattacks on America's networks and explains how the FCC is fighting back:

"This is a significant work stream at the FCC. We have a SCIF, a secure facility just down the hall from me here. I spend a lot of time in that."

"There’s this traditional foreign bad actors that are constantly looking to push and prod and work their way into our network infrastructure. But superintelligence is just gonna supercharge the ability of people to try to launch cyberattacks, and we’re very cognizant of that."

"President Trump has stood up the SI force. Scott Kupor’s got a piece of this from OPM, and Chairman Ferguson at the Federal Trade Commission has a piece of this."

"We just had a meeting on this, and we are working very hard on the stepwise challenges that superintelligence is gonna bring to securing our network."

"Historically, the mindset in government was, what is our authority? Let’s adopt rules and regulations. It’s a multi-year process. But that’s too slow. The attack vectors right now, powered by SI, change hourly and daily."

"We need to be in constant touch with C-suites telling, here’s what we’re seeing. What are you seeing? What change are you gonna make?"
@FCC

AI is literally saving lives right now:

• UC San Diego's AI sepsis model cut sepsis deaths by 17%.

• In a trial of 100,000+ women in Sweden, AI-supported screening found 29% more cancers.

• In a randomized trial involving 60,893 hospital encounters, an AI warning system reduced the hazard of in-hospital death by 35.6%.

• In a randomized trial of nearly 16,000 patients, AI-powered ECG alerts reduced 90-day mortality from 4.3% to 3.6%.

I've never seen technology this useful arrive this fast, and this is just the beginning.

These guys are doubling down:

You can now have agents working inside hospitals, learning from patients, helping doctors make decisions, and keeping the information secure.

items.title: Mercor's @edwardjhu reveals how AI benchmarks can reward models for guessing 10 different answers wh...
items.content:
Mercor's @edwardjhu reveals how AI benchmarks can reward models for guessing 10 different answers while penalizing others for getting it right:

"A rubric item might be, the final answer needs to be $3 million. Imagine the rubric item specifies it needs to be $300 million with two decimal points, and the model just said $3 million."

"Even though it’s numerically correct, because the rubric is overly specific, we’re failing the model in an unfair way."

"We released a benchmark called APEX Agents earlier this year, mirroring how a professional would actually work in front of a computer. Real professionals come up with legal or consulting tasks for the model to do over the course of 50 to 100 steps."

"One thing we noticed is that some models that are not in the top model family in terms of parameter size were doing much better than we expected. It turned out the model was doing what we call scattergunning. It will say, if A is true, it’s 2 million. If B is true, it’s 3 million. It might do it 10 times."

"As long as the model mentions 3 million, the LLM judge would say, awesome, you got it right."
@mercor
items.author: @MTSlive
items.summary: Mercor's Edward Hu explains benchmark fairness problems: overly specific rubrics unfairly fail numerically correct answers, and some models game benchmarks via scattergunning multiple conditional answers, rewarding guessing over correctness. He references the APEX Agents benchmark of 50-100 step professional tasks.
items.reasoning: Specific, original technical insight into benchmark gaming and rubric design from a benchmark builder, with decent engagement; echoes the broader benchmark-credibility debate in this batch.

items.title: Mercor's @edwardjhu reveals why researchers are designing AI benchmarks with tasks even humans can't...
items.content:
Mercor's @edwardjhu reveals why researchers are designing AI benchmarks with tasks even humans can't solve, just to make models fail:

"The benchmarks we have today are not gonna be good benchmarks in a year or two or even less."

"As the models become more capable, it’s increasingly hard to fail the model. And there is this tendency to fail the model at all costs, often at the expense of fairness or benchmark diversity."

"We’re asking the AI to do something that’s actually impossible, a human might not even be able to do it, or we find one way the model fails and we replicate it so many times"

"If the entire benchmark is testing just one failure mode, the benchmark score will swing from zero to near 100% very quickly. It’s easy for someone to look at a number and draw conclusions right away."

"But we really need to be thoughtful about the underlying design so that it’s not just a number people can cite, but a reliable instrument for the field."
@mercor

How do you assess cyclone risk beyond what a few decades of historical data can reveal?

@AXA researchers are using NVIDIA Earth-2 to help fill that gap.

Using FourCastNet 3, one of Earth-2’s open, global weather forecasting models, the team generated more than 1,000 simulated cyclone seasons to study possible storm activity around the globe.

items.title: ARC Prize President @GregKamradt explains why AI researchers could be among the last jobs automated:...
items.content:
ARC Prize President @GregKamradt explains why AI researchers could be among the last jobs automated:

"AI is very good at executing what you want it to do. It’s not very good at coming up with ideas. It’s not very good at coming up with hypotheses."

"We tried to make ARC-AGI-3 games with AI-generated ideas, and they’re all crap. They lacked the special substance about what we wanted."

"On the recent podcast with Dwarkesh, he was asking, what’s the last job people are gonna have? It was along the lines of AI researcher, because AI researcher’s gonna be the one to pose the good questions."

"A really good benchmark tests how well you’re able to come up with good questions, how well you’re able to come up with good hypotheses, with an uncapped ceiling."

"If you think about what society has done over the last thousand years, there’s no ceiling to the progress we’ve had. Clearly there’s a really good uncapped benchmark out there, and it’s our job to go and find it."
@arcprize

items.summary_html: ARC Prize President Greg Kamradt argues AI excels at execution but is poor at generating hypotheses, citing failed attempts at AI-generated ARC-AGI-3 game ideas, and suggests AI researchers may be among the last automated jobs because posing good questions remains hard; he frames finding an uncapped benchmark as the field's task.
items.content_html:
ARC Prize President @GregKamradt explains why AI researchers could be among the last jobs automated:

"AI is very good at executing what you want it to do. It’s not very good at coming up with ideas. It’s not very good at coming up with hypotheses."

"We tried to make ARC-AGI-3 games with AI-generated ideas, and they’re all crap. They lacked the special substance about what we wanted."

"On the recent podcast with Dwarkesh, he was asking, what’s the last job people are gonna have? It was along the lines of AI researcher, because AI researcher’s gonna be the one to pose the good questions."

"A really good benchmark tests how well you’re able to come up with good questions, how well you’re able to come up with good hypotheses, with an uncapped ceiling."

"If you think about what society has done over the last thousand years, there’s no ceiling to the progress we’ve had. Clearly there’s a really good uncapped benchmark out there, and it’s our job to go and find it."

@arcprize

items.title: ARC Prize President @GregKamradt explains why the final breakthrough to AGI might come from an entir...
items.content:
ARC Prize President @GregKamradt explains why the final breakthrough to AGI might come from an entirely different branch of AI research:

"Our job is to find benchmarks that humans can do and AI cannot, and that job is getting harder. It’s not impossible yet. We have plans for ARC 4."

"There’s two ideologies within the field right now. One is you’re gonna be able to create an RL environment for anything and just hill climb that forever."

"Capitalism is running a really big hill climbing experiment right now. The labs find a gap, the RL companies fill it, and you go back and forth."

"On the flip side is, once the algorithm to AGI is found and you have an actual human learner, that algorithm will be able to meta learn anything."

"ARC Prize, we’re more interested in almost the romantic pursuit of that general learner."

"I have a feeling it will be a different branch of the tech tree than what we’re currently going down. The shape of what we have right now will be like 98% of the solution, but then it’s gonna be a repackaging in some format that will bring us there."
@arcprize

items.title: MAI-Image-2.7-Preview scores higher than MAI-Image-2.6 on all 7 editing actions, and ranks #1 on 4 o...
items.content:
MAI-Image-2.7-Preview scores higher than MAI-Image-2.6 on all 7 editing actions, and ranks #1 on 4 of them

Our Image Arena taxonomy measures 7 editing actions and 10 use cases for Image Editing. Editing actions measure what an edit asks the model to do.

MAI-Image-2.7-Preview ranks #1 on Scene & Style Edit, Text or Symbol Edits, Reasoning-Based Edit, and Enhancement & Restoration. Its largest gains over MAI-Image-2.6 are in Composition & Framing, Text or Symbol Edits, and Scene & Style Edit. GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst (max) still scores higher on Composition & Framing, Object-Level Edit, and Identity Preserving Edit.

➤ Scene & Style Edit covers relighting, restyling, and changes to the background, setting, or overall treatment.

➤ Text or Symbol Edits covers editing text, typography, logos, and symbols within the image.

➤ Reasoning-Based Edit covers edits that need inference about the scene rather than a literal instruction.

items.title: Machenta CEO @Ed__Johns reveals how betting against the robotics industry's approach led his team to...
items.content:
Machenta CEO @Ed__Johns reveals how betting against the robotics industry's approach led his team to build robots that learn new tasks instantly from just one demonstration:

"I decided what I wanted to build is a robot brain that can learn tasks like a human. And the rest of the world went off in a different direction."

"They started collecting lots and lots of data in the real world, with the assumption that you would need to provide hundreds of demonstrations."

"I always thought there’s something not quite right about that, where a robot would need to spend hours or days to learn a task. That’s what I bet on at Imperial College."

"The internals of it are nothing like the human brain. But the way you interact with it is like interacting with a human."

"If I wanted to teach you a task, I could give you a demonstration, and you’d be able to do that task. You wouldn’t need hundreds of demonstrations, and you wouldn’t need days or weeks of training."

"You provide one demonstration of the task, and then instantly the robot will be able to perform that task. Which is very different to what’s been going on elsewhere in robotics, where the assumption has been that you need lots and lots of data to teach a robot even a basic task."
@Machenta_

items.title:
It’s been a few months now testing the @maticrobots vacuum cleaner

Before we had a Roborock (essent...
items.content:
It’s been a few months now testing the @maticrobots vacuum cleaner

Before we had a Roborock (essentially a Roomba knockoff)

But the Roborock became kinda useless, it'd always get stuck in any type of cable, it'd always get stuck not being able to get on to the thick rug, so you'd have to prep the room every single time just to use it

Too much work so we just stopped using it

The Matic is, well, completely different. It's not flat or low, it's a chunky tall kinda cute looking cube shaped thing with 2 big wheels

And it's a different philosophy, it has cameras and tries to understand its environment, more like a modern robot or a self driving Tesla than a classic Roomba-type vacuum

That makes it just way way better, it doesn't get stuck in cables, it doesn't get stuck in rugs, it drives and turns around the room almost like a mini car

It's also way more silent than Roborock or Roomba-type vacuums, and measurably way more powerful in both vacuuming and mopping

They also respond very fast to feedback and improve things fast, like companies should be these days (instead of getting stuck in some hellish corporate support flow)

Another thing, I don't trust consumer devices connected to the internet (and nor should you) so of course I asked to Claude to analyze if it was phoning home (remember the other vacuums who upload your house plan to China, that was true). Claude was conclusive, Matic never phoned home anything, excellent

Maybe the best part is, it just looks cute and you wanna anthropomorphize it, and they include 2 googly eye stickers so it becomes even more like a dog/cat/pet

@mehul made a great thing!

items.title:
I still have non-Brazilian friends who think São Paulo is fine to visit

We hired a great Uber drive...
items.content:
I still have non-Brazilian friends who think São Paulo is fine to visit

We hired a great Uber driver to drive us to Florianopolis, like a 3 hour trip, cause was easier than flying then, very nice guy

While driving I sat in the back talking a bit with him and practicing my Portuguese

Then I noticed he didn't wear a seatbelt so I asked why

He said "so I can draw my gun quickly"

I said "desculpa the fuck what gun"

Then he showed he was wearing a holster on his right side with a gun it which he carried for safety because he said drive into and out of São Paulo often

So being a funny naive Dutch guy I asked "so did you ever kill someone?"

He said "yes I killed a guy last year who came at me and who tried steal my car in São Paulo"

And then he told me he was in a judicial trial about it and being prosecuted for it 

I asked him again in the naive Dutch guy perspective "did you get like therapy after? like must be intense right, do you feel bad about that?

He said "no why? If I didn't kill him he would have killed me" ☠️ 

Foreigners especially Europeans have no clue how violent São Paulo and Rio are, it's just not in their mental framework to be able to understand the danger, Brazilians themselves are surprisingly honest and realistic about it

There a reason I stay the F out of São Paulo

I mpstly stick to South Brazil, it's safe, not as safe as Europe but mostly very safe and not really violent. The violence and crime there seems mostly isolated between gangs and in the few favelas there

About that too I asked Brazilians "why is South Brazil so safe?"

And they mostly agreed when a guy told me "because the police here shoot to kill" while in São Paulo and Rio the police is too scared to get prosecuted for killing people

items.content:
Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch): https://t.co/IzY3D4m8nG by @rasbt via @ManningBooks 
🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟
Amazon summary:

The book is especially useful because it implements the core methods from scratch rather than treating them as black-box library calls. Readers see how self-consistency, self-refinement, Best-of-N, and training-based methods actually work, including their cost and latency trade-offs. 

The book also discusses common failure modes, including cases where refinement can make answers worse. Difficult concepts such as softmax, temperature, and top-p sampling are clarified with code-linked explanations and diagrams, while visual workflows make pipelines and scoring methods easier to follow.

Reading the book feels like following a guided technical build rather than a loose survey of AI topics. Each concept is introduced because the project now needs it. Diagrams, roadmaps, code listings, exercises, and repeated workflow summaries help readers stay oriented through advanced material.

Machenta CEO @Ed__Johns explains how his team automated an entire assembly line in just 2 minutes, something that normally takes weeks or months:

"I decided I wanted to automate an entire assembly line. We put three robots side by side and created a task where the robots would package a box and then close the box, and each robot would do a different part of that task."

"I thought it’d be really cool if we could automate that whole thing in about two minutes, because traditionally automating an assembly line would take weeks or maybe even months of systems integration and manual programming. It’d be extremely expensive."

"If we could get instant robot learning working on an entire assembly line, this would be evidence of what the future of the manufacturing industry would look like."

"That’s one of my favorite tasks, an entire assembly line automated in two minutes."

"If we could get instant robot learning working on an entire assembly line, this would be evidence of what the future of the manufacturing industry would look like."

"That’s one of my favorite tasks, an entire assembly line automated in two minutes."

@Machenta_

Talked with my clanker and based on my nutrition I get about 200mg of magnesium per day

You need to get about 420mg per day, so I'm slightly deficient

About 60% of people are magnesium deficient and symptoms can be anxiety (and in turn bad sleep) because magnesium helps your brain regulate your nervous system and stress hormones like cortisol

I don't have any issues (no anxiety, no depression at all, mostly because regular gym and clean nutrition) but maybe good to take it to become even more chill

So I got Magnesium Glycinate supplements

I'll report back on the benefits! 😊 

One thing interesting is yeaaaars ago when I had lots of anxiety (before I started going gym and eating clean) I remember taking magnesium and my anxiety just disappeared, so it def works!

New release from @PacktPublishing, now available for preorder, with Amazon price guarantee at https://t.co/4nKKuY3nCJ

“Beyond LLMs — Learn how to design reliable AI systems with memory, agents, planning, control, and evaluation”

Amazon summary:

“Beyond LLMs” provides a practical way to understand and build the next generation of AI systems using Python. This book introduces you to the core ideas that sit beyond basic LLM usage, including memory, reasoning loops, planning, agents, control mechanisms, evaluation, monitoring, and hybrid constraints.

Using a recurring SupportOps AI project across the book, you will see how these capabilities fit together in a structured system rather than as isolated techniques. You will learn how to design modular components, measure reliability and drift, handle failure modes, and make safer update decisions as the system evolves.

By the end of the book, you will be able to move from prompt-driven demos to more reliable, production-ready AI systems that are easier to test, monitor, and improve.

AI and the Octopus Organization — Building the Superintelligent Firm: https://t.co/4VwzCr0jiM

AMAZO...
items.content:
AI and the Octopus Organization — Building the Superintelligent Firm: https://t.co/4VwzCr0jiM

AMAZON SUMMARY:

This is not another book about chatbots or automation. It’s a deeply researched, vividly told blueprint for transforming businesses so that they can make the most of AI. The secrets explored include what skills to cultivate, how to excel with human + AI combinations, how to organize teams for maximum impact, and how to deal with the emotional side of AI-driven change. This book is a practical guide to shaping an AI business strategy for executives who need to lead at scale without losing agility. The book describes how AI is already reshaping growth, coordination, and culture, providing an actionable roadmap to what the authors call the Octopus Organization™, one that can navigate the change ahead.

Backed by over two million data points from workforce surveys, insights from 50+ global leaders, and fresh 2026 real-world case studies from companies like HelloFresh, BBVA, Mass General Brigham, Siemens, and Procter & Gamble, the book “AI and the Octopus Organization” reveals how your company can:
• Empower the frontline with AI-enhanced autonomy
• Create networks for decision-making across silos
• Rapidly adapt to disruptions without losing control
• Build a culture that embraces experimentation
• Replace old approaches with superintelligent coordination
